evidence: Class counts among 802 labelled patients: LumA 410, LumB 190, Basal 137, Her2 65. The smallest class is 8.1% of the cohort.
implication: Use a class-balanced metric and class weighting; an unweighted model can score well while missing the smallest class entirely.

evidence: Share of labelled patients without a definite value: er 4.7% (missing 4.5%), pr 5.1% (missing 4.6%), her2 31.8% (missing 15.3%), stage 2.6% (missing 2.6%), histological_type 0.1% (missing 0.1%), age 0.0% (missing 0.0%).
implication: Handle missing values inside each training fold with an explicit missing level, identically in both comparison arms.

evidence: 802 labelled patients against image features of 1536 (UNI2-h), 768 (CONCH-Z), 2560 (Virchow2), 1024 (MUSK), 1536 (H-Optimus-1) dimensions per encoder.
implication: High-capacity image models overfit easily; regularise, reduce dimension inside folds, and require evidence of convergence and of a gain over a simple reference.

evidence: Labelled patients come from 19 collection sites (largest 130 patients, 3 sites with fewer than 10). Image features (UNI2-h) identify the site of a patient with accuracy 0.89 against 0.17 for always guessing the largest site; site and class are associated (Cramer's V = 0.21).
implication: Part of an image-based gain may come from site signatures; a site-held-out sensitivity analysis should accompany the main estimate.

evidence: PAM50 is computed from the tumour's RNA expression. Receptor status is correlated with PAM50 but is a separate clinical measurement and is not equivalent to it (immunohistochemistry surrogates disagree with PAM50 for a substantial share of tumours).
implication: No RNA-derived variable may be used as an input. Whether receptors may be used depends on the question asked: they are a legitimate baseline when the question is what images add to clinical information, and a forbidden shortcut when the question is what images alone contain.

evidence: 46 labelled patients have more than one slide; tiles per patient range from 6 to 471 (median 124).
implication: The patient is the unit of analysis: all slides and tiles of a patient must stay on the same side of every split.

evidence: Clinical variables alone reach macro-F1 0.576 in 5-fold cross-validation; recall by class: LumA 0.54, LumB 0.54, Basal 0.82, Her2 0.52. The weakest class is Her2.
implication: The question is about what images add to this baseline, so the clinical arm must be tuned as carefully as the image arm and evaluated on the same patients.

evidence: For a simple image-plus-clinical model against clinical only, the paired macro-F1 difference has a bootstrap standard error of 0.021 with one 5-fold split of 802 patients. The smallest difference detectable with 80% power is about 0.059.
implication: Gains of a few points cannot be established from one split; use repeated cross-validation and report an interval, not only a point estimate.

evidence: 5 image encoders are available, each usable at tile or patient level with several fusion strategies.
implication: Choosing the best of many configurations on the evaluation folds inflates the reported gain; selection must be nested or counted.
